newsitem.title: USA: Consumer confidence seen stable in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Consumer confidence seen stable in 1997.

text.p: Buoyed by strong job prospects, Americans are still optimistic about the economy, which should lead to another year of solid spending on homes and vehicles, a University of Michigan survey said Thursday.

Consumers expect unemployment to remain low, inflation to stay in check and remain unconcerned about their current debt loads, said Richard Curtin, director of the university's consumer survey unit, which publishes a closely watched monthly consumer confidence guide.
"We can certainly expect one more year of growth," Curtin said at the university 44th annual economic conference.

The average for the consumer sentiment index so far this year is 92.7, up slightly from the 92.3 average in 1995, Curtin said. Three years in a row of readings in the low 90s rivals the level of optimism of the 1980s, he said.
Consumers do not see a big jump in their fortunes. Rather, their generally upbeat mood is based on more than five years of economic expansion and a belief that things will continue.
"The only concern that consumers have when they look ahead is they expect interest rates to rise. But at this point, they expect the increase to be rather modest," he said.
Except for interest rate expectations, Curtin's findings are in line with the annual economic forecast for 1997-98 delivered by University of Michigan Professor Saul Hymans.

According to Hymans, the economy will grow at a modest 2.4 percent rate in 1997 and 2.3 percent in 1998, essentially unchanged from the 2.5 percent forecast for the fourth quarter of 1996. Consumer prices are seen rising two percent and 2.4 percent over the next two years.
Unemployment is forecast at 5.3 percent next year and 5.4 percent in 1998, compared to 5.2 percent in October. The slight rise is based on an assumption that productivity will improve, Hymans said.
Hymans sees relatively little change in short and long-term interest rates over the next two years.

The biggest danger ahead is if productivity continues to lag. If that occurs and demand keeps growing, he said, higher wage costs could lead to higher prices and a pickup in inflation, which could force the Federal Reserve to raise short-term interest rates.
